To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) ALMA blind observations of the ALPINES survey allow us to sample the faint end of the IR luminosity function up to high redshift, and to identify luminous and massive dusty galaxies that would otherwise be missed by the optical/near-IR surveys; (ii) the IR LF does not evolve significantly from z~2 to z~6, and the SFRD remains almost constant up to z=4.
ALMA has detected 56 continuum sources serendipitous in the ALPINE survey.

the ALMA [CII]-detected sources in the ALPINE blind survey are the first to sample the faint end of the infrared LF up to z~5.5, and that the contribution of dusty star formation to the cosmic SFRD is significantly higher than previously thought.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of galaxies at high redshift, and in particular of their star formation history and evolution.
the nature of dusty galaxies at the highest redshift.
the nature and properties of the optically dark population, and their impact on the total SFR and stellar mass budget at high-z.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the ALPINE blind survey has unveiled a population of massive and luminous dusty star-forming galaxies that were previously hidden in the far-infrared, and that dominate the SFRD and the high-mass tail of the stellar mass functions at the highest redshift probed.

ALPINE seredipitous sources are not a representative sample of the general galaxy population, and that they are not a good proxy of the general population of star-forming galaxies at z>3, but they are a very interesting and important sample to study the extreme and rare dusty galaxies at z>4, with high luminosities and high stellar masses, that would have been missed in the general surveys.
the ALPINE survey is the first blind far-infrared survey to probe the faint-end of infrared LF and the SFRD up to z~5, and to detect optically+near/near-IR dark galaxies up to z=5.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the total SFR density at high-z is dominated by dusty star formation, which is not well traced by UV/optical surveys, while the most massive galaxies at high redshift are optically dark, with the bulk of their star formation obscured by dust.
the [CII] emission is a very powerful tool for studying the nature, the evolution and the SFRD of the most luminous galaxies up to z=5.
the [CII] emission is a very powerful tool to trace obscured star formation up the highest redshift.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, while the total SFR is dominated by the optically bright population, a significant contribution to the SFR density at z=5 is coming from dusty galaxies that are not detected in any other wavebands.
a significant fraction of the SFRD is produced by galaxies that are missed in the optical/near-IR surveys, and that are not detected in the [CII] line.

the [CII] emission line is a powerful probe to detect obscured galaxies up to z>6, and that the contribution of dusty galaxies to the cosmic star formation history at high-z is not negligible.
